Someone else's finger can make you squirm. Your own finger, same spot, feels dull.
That's because your brain predicts its own touch.
Every time you move, it sends a copy of the command, a forecast of what you'll feel, and turns that feeling down.
In 1998, brain scans showed it: the touch area reacted less to people's own touch than to one they didn't make.
Then the team got clever. People moved a robot arm that stroked their own palm.
Add a delay of a fifth of a second, or twist the direction, and the same touch felt more ticklish.
The forecast missed, so the brain treated it as the outside world.
So a tickle is really about surprise. Your brain feels what it didn't see coming.
